orientation.theme: Whether age at first MMR vaccination is associated with autism overall or in potentially susceptible subgroups.
orientation.thesis: In this metropolitan Atlanta case-control study, children with autism and matched controls had similar ages at first MMR vaccination, with no association before 18 or 24 months, including regression subgroups; the observed before-36-month association is likely an artifact of special-education immunization requirements rather than evidence that MMR causes autism.

thesisHinge.proposition: Earlier MMR vaccination before the clinically relevant 18- and 24-month cutoffs was not more common among autism cases than matched controls.

grounding.verbatimExcerpt: Vaccination before 36 months was more common among case children than control children, especially among children 3 to 5 years of age, likely reflecting immunization requirements for enrollment in early intervention programs. Rather than representing causal relationships, associations with the 36-month cutoff would be more likely than associations with earlier age cutoffs to have been influenced by factors related to the evaluation, management, and treatment of the child. For example, case children might have been more likely than control children to have been vaccinated as a requirement for enrollment in early intervention or preschool special education programs. This possibility is supported by the finding that the difference between case and control children in the proportion vaccinated before 36 months of age was strongest in the 3- to 5-year-old age group. The difference in vaccination coverage by 36 months of age between case and control children is likely to be an artifact of immunization requirements for preschool special education attendance in case children.

argumentUnits.canonicalAtomicProposition: The higher before-36-month vaccination rate among autism cases likely reflects vaccination requirements for early-intervention or preschool special-education enrollment rather than a causal effect of MMR.
